children.title: Locally Lipschitz Nonsmooth Problem Class
children.top_down_role: The principal finite-dimensional class for Clarke-based sampling and stationarity complexity.

knowledge_statements.title: Locally Lipschitz Nonsmooth Problem Class
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional, unconstrained locally Lipschitz objectives with Clarke generalized derivatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A locally Lipschitz nonsmooth problem in this class is \(\min_{x\in U} f(x)\), where \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is open and \(f:U\to\mathbb{R}\) satisfies the following condition: for every \(x\in U\), there exist a neighborhood \(V\subseteq U\) of \(x\) and a constant \(L_V<\infty\) such that \[|f(y)-f(z)|\leq L_V\lVert y-z\rVert\qquad\text{for all }y,z\in V.\] Such an \(f\) is differentiable almost everywhere in \(U\), and its Clarke directional derivative and Clarke subdifferential are defined at every \(x\in U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This problem class minimizes a finite-valued, locally Lipschitz objective on an open finite-dimensional domain. Such an objective is differentiable almost everywhere and admits Clarke generalized derivatives at every point of the domain.
assumptions_latex: The objective is finite-valued on an open set \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The local Lipschitz property makes the Clarke directional derivative and Clarke subdifferential well-defined at every \(x\in U\).

notation.meaning: Clarke subdifferential of the objective at a point

children.title: Directional Semidifferentiable Models
children.top_down_role: Models whose computational structure is expressed through directional semidifferentiability.

assumptions_latex: The function is finite-valued on an open set \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Directional semidifferentiability at \(x\) means that every fixed-direction, one-sided first-order quotient has a finite limit.

notation.meaning: One-sided directional derivative at a point in a direction

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-direction, one-sided directional semidifferentiability in finite dimensions.

source_refs.locator: 4.1.1 Generalized directional derivatives p. 159

source_refs.locator: 3.1.1 Generalized Directional Derivative p. 61

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(f:U\to\mathbb{R}\) is directionally semidifferentiable at \(x\in U\) when, for every \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the finite one-sided limit \[f'(x;d):=\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{f(x+td)-f(x)}{t}\] exists. It is directionally semidifferentiable on \(U\) when this condition holds at every \(x\in U\). The definition fixes \(d\) while \(t\) tends to zero and therefore does not, by itself, require stability under perturbations of the direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A model is directionally semidifferentiable when its finite one-sided derivative exists along every fixed direction; robustness to varying directions is not included.
knowledge_statements.title: Directional Semidifferentiable Models

children.title: Hadamard Semidifferentiable Models
children.top_down_role: Models using the stronger perturbation-stable semidifferentiability regime.

assumptions_latex: The function is finite-valued on an open set \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Hadamard semidifferentiability requires a common directional limit under simultaneous perturbation of step sizes and directions.

notation.meaning: Hadamard directional derivative at a point in a direction
Perturbed direction converging to the target direction

knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-sided Hadamard semidifferentiability for real-valued finite-dimensional models.

source_refs.locator: 4.1.1 Generalized directional derivatives p. 159
source_refs.source_title: Modern Nonconvex Nondifferentiable Optimization

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(f:U\to\mathbb{R}\) is Hadamard semidifferentiable at \(x\in U\) if, for every \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\), there exists a finite value \(f'_H(x;d)\) satisfying \[f'_H(x;d)=\lim_{\substack{t\downarrow0\\ d'\to d}}\frac{f(x+td')-f(x)}{t}.\] Equivalently, every pair of sequences \(t_k\downarrow0\) and \(d_k\to d\), with \(x+t_kd_k\in U\), yields the same quotient limit. This condition is stronger than existence of fixed-direction derivatives alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hadamard semidifferentiability requires the one-sided directional quotient to converge even when the direction is perturbed as the step vanishes.
knowledge_statements.title: Hadamard Semidifferentiable Models

children.title: Chain-Rule Compatibility Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regimes where semidifferentiable structure supports compositional computational analysis.

assumptions_latex: The inner mapping \(F:U\to\mathbb{R}^m\) is Hadamard semidifferentiable at \(x\).
The outer function \(g:V\to\mathbb{R}\) is Hadamard semidifferentiable at \(F(x)\), where \(F(U)\subseteq V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The composite \(g\circ F\) is Hadamard semidifferentiable at \(x\) and obeys the directional chain rule.

notation.meaning: Hadamard semiderivative of the inner mapping

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Hadamard chain rule for a scalar outer function.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Nonsmooth Analysis p. 149
source_refs.source_title: Modern Nonconvex Nondifferentiable Optimization

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A chain-rule-compatible regime holds at \(x\in U\) when \(F:U\to\mathbb{R}^m\) is Hadamard semidifferentiable at \(x\), \(g:V\to\mathbb{R}\) is Hadamard semidifferentiable at \(F(x)\), and \(F(U)\subseteq V\). Then \(h:=g\circ F\) is Hadamard semidifferentiable at \(x\), and for every \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \[h'_H(x;d)=g'_H\bigl(F(x);F'_H(x;d)\bigr).\] Thus the propagated inner semiderivative must lie in the direction domain on which the outer semiderivative is defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hadamard semidifferentiability of compatible inner and outer mappings yields a semidifferentiable composite whose derivative is obtained by directional composition.
knowledge_statements.title: Chain-Rule Compatibility Regimes

children.title: Finite-Max Models
children.top_down_role: Objectives represented through finitely many smooth component functions.

assumptions_latex: The index set \(I=\{1,\ldots,m\}\) is finite.
Each component \(f_i:U\to\mathbb{R}\) is continuously differentiable on the open set \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The maximum model is locally Lipschitz, and its Clarke subdifferential is the convex hull of gradients of active components.

notation.meaning: Indices attaining the maximum at a point

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite maxima of continuously differentiable real-valued component functions.

source_refs.locator: 7.2.1 Piecewise smooth functions p. 656
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite-max model has the representation \[f(x)=\max_{i\in I}f_i(x),\qquad I=\{1,\ldots,m\},\] with active index set \[I(x):=\{i\in I:f_i(x)=f(x)\}.\] If every \(f_i\) is continuously differentiable on \(U\), then \(f\) is locally Lipschitz on \(U\), its directional derivative satisfies \[f'(x;d)=\max_{i\in I(x)}\langle\nabla f_i(x),d\rangle,\] and its Clarke subdifferential is \[\partial_C f(x)=\operatorname{conv}\{\nabla f_i(x):i\in I(x)\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-max objective is the maximum of finitely many smooth components; active component gradients determine its directional derivative and Clarke subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Max Models

children.title: Piecewise-Smooth Models
children.top_down_role: Objectives organized by smooth pieces across local regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Piecewise-Smooth Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Locally finite continuous selections from continuously differentiable functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A continuous function \(f:U\to\mathbb{R}\), where \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is open, is piecewise smooth if, for every \(x\in U\), there exist a neighborhood \(V\subseteq U\) of \(x\) and finitely many continuously differentiable functions \(f_1,\ldots,f_m:V\to\mathbb{R}\) such that \[f(y)\in\{f_1(y),\ldots,f_m(y)\}\qquad\text{for every }y\in V.\] Every function satisfying this local finite-selection definition is locally Lipschitz on \(U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous piecewise-smooth model locally coincides pointwise with one of finitely many continuously differentiable selection functions and is consequently locally Lipschitz.
assumptions_latex: The domain \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is open.
A finite family of continuously differentiable selection functions is available locally around every point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A piecewise-smooth model locally equals one of finitely many smooth selections and is therefore locally Lipschitz.

children.title: Active-Piece Representation Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Computational access to locally relevant smooth pieces.

assumptions_latex: The objective has a known finite family of differentiable local pieces.
Queries are restricted to points where the requested active pieces are differentiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The interface exposes precisely the active values and gradients needed to construct local generalized-gradient candidates.

notation.meaning: Active piece indices returned at a query point
Gradient of active piece indexed by i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic query interface for explicitly represented finite-piece objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a query point \(x\), an active-piece interface returns \[\mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{act}}(x)=\bigl(f(x),I(x),\{f_i(x),\nabla f_i(x):i\in I(x)\}\bigr),\] where \(I(x)\) contains exactly the represented pieces attaining or selecting \(f(x)\). Initialization consists of supplying the finite piece representation and its evaluation routines. A query evaluates the pieces, identifies \(I(x)\), and returns the displayed data. Sampling algorithms may stop after a prescribed query budget or stationarity test and output the convex hull of collected active gradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each query, the interface identifies the represented active pieces and returns their values and gradients for generalized-gradient construction.
knowledge_statements.title: Active-Piece Representation Interfaces

Each component depends only on a specified subset of coordinates and is piecewise smooth on its reduced space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The objective decomposes into low-dimensional nonsmooth components whose local discrete-gradient contributions can be assembled componentwise.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A piecewise partially separable objective has the representation \[f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m f_i(P_i x),\] where each \(P_i:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^{n_i}\) selects or linearly combines only the coordinates used by component \(i\), typically with \(n_i\ll n\), and each \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^{n_i}\to\mathbb{R}\) is piecewise smooth. Function differences caused by a coordinate perturbation can therefore be computed by reevaluating only components whose maps \(P_i\) involve that coordinate, permitting componentwise assembly of discrete-gradient information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A piecewise partially separable objective sums low-dimensional piecewise-smooth components, so coordinate perturbations require reevaluating only affected components.

children.title: ReLU Network Objectives
children.top_down_role: Piecewise-defined network objectives motivating practical oracle models.

assumptions_latex: The network has finitely many layers and finite-dimensional parameters.
Hidden units use the ReLU activation and the empirical loss is locally Lipschitz in network outputs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The empirical objective is locally Lipschitz in the parameters and is smooth on each fixed activation-pattern stratum.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite feedforward ReLU networks with locally Lipschitz empirical losses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For data \((a_j,b_j)_{j=1}^N\), a ReLU network objective has the form \[L(\theta)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^N \ell\bigl(F_\theta(a_j),b_j\bigr)+r(\theta),\] where each hidden layer applies \(\sigma(t)=\max\{0,t\}\) componentwise. If \(\ell\) and \(r\) are locally Lipschitz, then \(L\) is locally Lipschitz. On every open parameter region where all preactivation signs for the data are fixed, the ReLU gates are fixed; consequently, \(L\) is differentiable there whenever \(\ell\) and \(r\) are differentiable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A ReLU training objective is locally Lipschitz and becomes smooth on parameter regions having a fixed activation pattern, assuming smooth loss and regularization there.
knowledge_statements.title: ReLU Network Objectives

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No citation is supplied, and the conclusion asserts smoothness on fixed activation strata although the assumptions require only locally Lipschitz losses. The statement itself adds differentiability conditions not present in the assumptions or conclusion.

children.title: Margin-Based Learning Objectives
children.top_down_role: Nonsmooth classification models used in near-stationarity studies.

assumptions_latex: The dataset \((a_j,y_j)_{j=1}^N\) is finite with labels \(y_j\in\{-1,1\}\).
The score map \(s_\theta(a)\) and regularizer \(r(\theta)\) are locally Lipschitz in \(\theta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The hinge-loss empirical objective is locally Lipschitz and nonsmooth where one or more signed margins equal one.

notation.meaning: Signed classification margin for sample j

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary empirical risk with hinge loss and a locally Lipschitz regularizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A margin-based hinge objective is represented by \[L(\theta)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^N[1-y_j s_\theta(a_j)]_+ + r(\theta),\qquad [t]_+:=\max\{0,t\}.\] If every score \(s_\theta(a_j)\) and \(r\) is locally Lipschitz in \(\theta\), then \(L\) is locally Lipschitz. Its loss term is nonsmooth at parameters satisfying \(y_j s_\theta(a_j)=1\) for at least one sample. For affine scores and smooth \(r\), the objective is finite-max or piecewise smooth.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A hinge-loss objective penalizes margins below one; it is locally Lipschitz and is nonsmooth at samples lying exactly on the unit-margin boundary.
knowledge_statements.title: Margin-Based Learning Objectives

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No citation supports the selected hinge-loss variant. Equality of a margin to one identifies a possible kink but does not by itself guarantee that the composite objective is nonsmooth without nondegeneracy assumptions on the score map.

children.title: Differentiable-Point Gradient Oracle
children.top_down_role: Gradient access on smooth strata of an almost-everywhere differentiable objective.

assumptions_latex: The objective \(f:U\to\mathbb{R}\) is locally Lipschitz on an open set \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\).
Queries are made only at differentiability points of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each successful query returns the classical gradient, which is an admissible local gradient sample for Clarke-subdifferential approximation.

notation.meaning: Set of differentiability points of the objective

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact deterministic gradient access on the full-measure differentiability set.

source_refs.locator: 7.1 Nonsmooth Analysis I: Clarke's Calculus p. 626
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D_f\subseteq U\) denote the set where \(f\) is classically differentiable. The oracle accepts \(z\in D_f\) and returns \[\mathcal{O}_{\nabla}(z)=\bigl(f(z),\nabla f(z)\bigr).\] A sampling procedure initializes a center \(x\) and radius \(\delta>0\), draws or selects points \(z_k\in D_f\cap B(x,\delta)\), queries their gradients, and stops after its prescribed sample budget or stationarity test. Its output may be any declared aggregate of the sampled gradients, commonly their convex hull or its minimum-norm element.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The oracle returns the exact value and classical gradient at differentiability points, allowing nearby gradients to approximate Clarke generalized-gradient information.
knowledge_statements.title: Differentiable-Point Gradient Oracle

children.title: Generalized-Subgradient Selection Oracle
children.top_down_role: An idealized generalized-gradient interface used in oracle-complexity analysis.

assumptions_latex: The objective \(f:U\to\mathbb{R}\) is locally Lipschitz.
A specified generalized subdifferential \(\partial f(x)\) is nonempty at every admissible query point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each query returns one valid but otherwise unspecified element of the chosen generalized subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ideal exact selection oracle for a declared generalized subdifferential.

source_refs.locator: 7.1 Nonsmooth Analysis I: Clarke's Calculus p. 626
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a generalized subdifferential mapping \(x\mapsto\partial f(x)\), such as the Clarke subdifferential. At an admissible query point \(x\in U\), the selection oracle returns \[\mathcal{O}_{\partial}(x)=\bigl(f(x),g_x\bigr),\qquad g_x\in\partial f(x).\] The selection may depend on the oracle and need not expose the entire set. An algorithm initializes its iterate, repeatedly chooses query points from previous outputs, and stops according to a declared budget or stationarity rule; its output is the final iterate and any collected selections required by that rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The idealized oracle returns the objective value and one unspecified valid element of a declared generalized subdifferential at each query.
knowledge_statements.title: Generalized-Subgradient Selection Oracle

children.top_down_role: Differentiable-point gradients coupled with explicit handling of nonsmooth query points.

children.title: Differentiable-Point Gradient Queries
children.top_down_role: Gradient information available at differentiable query points.

assumptions_latex: \(f:U\to\mathbb{R}\) is locally Lipschitz on an open set \(U\subset\mathbb{R}^n\).
The queried point \(y\in U\) is a differentiability point of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G_f(y)=\nabla f(y)\).

notation.meaning: Classical gradient of the objective at the query point

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact-gradient interface restricted to differentiability points of a locally Lipschitz objective.

source_refs.locator: 7.1 Nonsmooth Analysis I: Clarke's Calculus p. 626

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A differentiable-point gradient query is a partial oracle \(G_f:\operatorname{dom}G_f\to\mathbb{R}^n\), where \(\operatorname{dom}G_f=\{y\in U:f\text{ is Fréchet differentiable at }y\}\), whose response satisfies \(G_f(y)=\nabla f(y)\). The interface makes no prescribed vector response when \(y\notin\operatorname{dom}G_f\); an implementation may instead return a distinguished failure status.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a point where the locally Lipschitz objective is differentiable, the query returns its classical gradient; behavior at a nonsmooth point is explicitly unspecified or flagged.

children.title: Nonsmooth-Point Detection
children.top_down_role: Oracle signaling for query points lacking an ordinary gradient.

assumptions_latex: The interface exposes only function values and differentiable-point gradients at finitely many adaptively chosen points.
The objective class contains all locally Lipschitz functions on a neighborhood of the tested point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No such finite-query procedure decides differentiability at \(x\) correctly for every objective in the class.

notation.meaning: Point whose differentiability is to be decided

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Black-box limitation for exact detection from finitely many local observations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every finite query set \(Q\subset U\) and every deterministic decision based on the observed values and available gradients on \(Q\), there exist locally Lipschitz functions \(f_0,f_1:U\to\mathbb{R}\) producing identical observations on \(Q\), while \(f_0\) is differentiable at \(x\) and \(f_1\) is not differentiable at \(x\). Hence a returned nonsmooth status requires additional structural evidence, such as a failed derivative evaluation or a detected switching boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite black-box values and gradients cannot universally decide differentiability; reliable nonsmooth detection needs extra structural or implementation evidence.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonsmooth-Point Detection

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The universal indistinguishability claim fails when the finite query set contains x and the interface exposes whether a gradient is available: differentiability of f0 at x and nondifferentiability of f1 at x then produce distinguishable availability outcomes. No source is supplied for a narrower valid impossibility theorem.

children.title: Query-Point Perturbation Policies
children.top_down_role: Policies for relocating queries when nonsmooth points are encountered.

assumptions_latex: \(f:U\to\mathbb{R}\) is locally Lipschitz and \(x\in U\).
The sampling distribution is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure and supported in \(B(x,\varepsilon)\subset U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{P}(Y\in D_f)=1\), where \(D_f\) is the differentiability set of \(f\).

children.title: Stochastic First-Order Oracle
children.top_down_role: Random or noisy first-order information used in stochastic stationarity methods.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is locally Lipschitz.
The oracle randomness \(\xi\) is sampled conditionally on the query point \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}[G(x,\xi)\mid x]\in\partial_C f(x)\) and \(\mathbb{E}[\|G(x,\xi)\|^2\mid x]\le M^2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unbiased-in-mean Clarke first-order oracle with bounded conditional second moment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A stochastic first-order oracle for \(f\) is a measurable map \((x,\xi)\mapsto G(x,\xi)\in\mathbb{R}^n\) such that, for every admissible \(x\), the conditional mean exists and satisfies \(\mathbb{E}[G(x,\xi)\mid x]\in\partial_C f(x)\), while \(\mathbb{E}[\|G(x,\xi)\|^2\mid x]\le M^2\) for a finite constant \(M\). A query returns an independent realization of \(G(x,\xi)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stochastic first-order query returns a random vector whose conditional mean is a Clarke subgradient and whose conditional second moment is uniformly bounded.

children.title: Value-Only Sampling Oracle

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A value-only sampling oracle for \(f\) is the map \(V_f:U\to\mathbb{R}\) defined by \(V_f(y)=f(y)\). Randomized smoothing methods may choose \(Y\) randomly, but exactness here refers to the returned values conditional on the chosen points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The oracle returns exact function values at requested sample points and provides no derivative information; the sampling locations may themselves be randomized.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_m=\operatorname{conv}\{v_1,\ldots,v_m\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An existential assertion
\[
\inf_{\|y-x\|\le\delta}\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial_C f(y))\le\varepsilon
\]
does not constitute recovered witness data unless the output includes \((y,g)\) satisfying \(\|y-x\|\le\delta\), \(g\in\partial_C f(y)\), and \(\|g\|\le\varepsilon\). children.title: GAS–NAS Separation
children.top_down_role: The gap between neighborhood convexification and existence of a nearby small-subgradient witness.

assumptions_latex: \(f(s,t)=e^s\cos t\) on \(\mathbb R^2\).
The reported point is \(x=(0,0)\) and the radius is \(\delta=\pi\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\in\partial_{\pi}f(x)\), but \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial_C f(y))\ge e^{-\pi}\) for every \(y\in\overline B(x,\pi)\).

notation.meaning: Goldstein neighborhood subdifferential at radius pi

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the displayed gradient calculation directly verifies the separation
constructed counterexample lacks an external source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A smooth two-dimensional example separates neighborhood convexification from any nearby small-gradient witness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f(s,t)=e^s\cos t\),
\[
\nabla f(s,t)=e^s(\cos t,-\sin t),
\qquad \|\nabla f(s,t)\|=e^s>0.
\]
The points \((0,0)\) and \((0,\pi)\) lie in \(\overline B((0,0),\pi)\), and their gradients are \((1,0)\) and \((-1,0)\). Hence their midpoint gives \(0\in\partial_{\pi}f(0,0)\), so the Goldstein residual is zero. However, every \((s,t)\) in that ball has \(s\ge-\pi\), whence \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial_C f(s,t))=\|\nabla f(s,t)\|\ge e^{-\pi}\). Therefore no \((\pi,\varepsilon)\) nearby stationary witness exists when \(\varepsilon<e^{-\pi}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth function can have cancelling gradients across a neighborhood, giving exact Goldstein stationarity while every individual nearby gradient remains bounded away from zero.
knowledge_statements.title: GAS–NAS Separation

knowledge_statements.title: Local Random Sampling Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absolutely continuous local sampling that almost surely selects differentiability points; no claim of complete gradient-regime coverage is made.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be an open set of full Lebesgue measure on which \(f\) is continuously differentiable, and let \(\varepsilon>0\). Draw \(y_1,\ldots,y_m\) independently from distributions whose densities are positive almost everywhere on \(B(x,\varepsilon)\). Then \[\mathbb{P}\!\left(y_i\in D\text{ for all }i=1,\ldots,m\right)=1.\] Consequently, \(\nabla f(y_i)\) is almost surely defined for every random sample. The condition \(m\ge n+1\) allows a collection of enough vectors to form a full-dimensional hull in \(\mathbb{R}^n\), but does not guarantee that the sampled gradients span such a hull or represent every locally active gradient regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Continuous local sampling selects differentiability points almost surely. Having at least n+1 samples allows, but does not guarantee, a full-dimensional sampled-gradient hull or coverage of all local gradient regimes.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is locally Lipschitz near \(x\).
There is an open set \(D\) of full Lebesgue measure on which \(f\) is continuously differentiable.
\(m\ge n+1\), \(\varepsilon>0\), and the samples are independent with densities positive almost everywhere on \(B(x,\varepsilon)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: With probability one, every random sample lies in \(D\), so every sampled gradient is defined; full-dimensional sampled-gradient coverage is not guaranteed.

children.title: Gradient-Sampling Stationarity Subproblem
children.top_down_role: Minimum-norm aggregation over the sampled-gradient hull.

knowledge_statements.title: Gradient-Sampling Stationarity Subproblem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean minimum-norm element of the finite sampled-gradient hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For sampled gradients \(q_0,\ldots,q_m\in\mathbb{R}^n\), define \(G:=\operatorname{conv}\{q_0,ldots,q_m\}\), \(Q:=[q_0\ \cdots\ q_m]\), and \(\Delta_{m+1}:=\{\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^{m+1}:\lambda\ge0,\ \mathbf{1}^{\mathsf T}\lambda=1\}\). The stationarity subproblem is \[\min_{g\in G}\frac12\|g\|^2=\min_{\lambda\in\Delta_{m+1}}\frac12\|Q\lambda\|^2.\] Its aggregate \(g^*=P_G(0)\) is unique, although an optimal representing weight can be nonunique. A vector \(\lambda^*\in\Delta_{m+1}\) is optimal exactly when \(Q\lambda^*=g^*\) and \(\langle q_i-g^*,g^*\rangle\ge0\) for every \(i=0,\ldots,m\). The sampled stationarity residual is \(\|g^*\|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The stationarity subproblem computes the unique minimum-norm vector in the sampled-gradient hull through a simplex-constrained convex quadratic program; its representing weights need not be unique.
assumptions_latex: The vectors \(q_0,\ldots,q_m\in\mathbb{R}^n\) are available sampled gradients.
The feasible weights belong to \(\Delta_{m+1}:=\{\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^{m+1}:\lambda\ge0,\ \mathbf{1}^{\mathsf T}\lambda=1\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The unique minimum-norm aggregate is \(g^*=P_G(0)=Q\lambda^*\), where \(\lambda^*\) solves the stated convex quadratic program.

knowledge_statements.title: Sampled Descent Directions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Descent is certified for the finite sampled linear model, not automatically for the objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=\operatorname{conv}\{q_0,\ldots,q_m\}\subset\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(g=P_G(0)\ne0\), and set \(d:=-g\). Then \[\langle v,d\rangle\le-\|g\|^2<0\qquad\text{for every }v\in G.\] In particular, \(\langle q_i,d\rangle\le-\|g\|^2\) for every sampled gradient \(q_i\). For the normalized direction \(\widehat d:=-g/\|g\|\), \(\langle q_i,\widehat d\rangle\le-\|g\|\). These inequalities certify descent for the sampled linear models only; objective-function decrease requires a globalization test.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The negative minimum-norm sampled aggregate is a common strict descent direction for every gradient in the sampled hull, but objective decrease still requires globalization.

children.title: Fixed-Radius Neighborhood Stationarity
children.top_down_role: Convergence and termination behavior at persistent sampling resolution.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is locally Lipschitz near \(x_*\).
\(x_k\to x_*\), \(\varepsilon_k\to\bar\varepsilon>0\), and \(\|g_k\|\le\nu_k\to\bar\nu\).
The sampled hulls \(G_k\) converge in Hausdorff distance to a compact convex neighborhood-gradient hull \(G_{\bar\varepsilon}(x_*)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The limit satisfies \(\operatorname{dist}(0,G_{\bar\varepsilon}(x_*))\le\bar\nu\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional Hausdorff-consistency form of fixed-radius neighborhood stationarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(k\), let \(g_k=P_{G_k}(0)\). If \(G_k\) converges in Hausdorff distance to \(G_{\bar\varepsilon}(x_*)\), then continuity of distance under compact-set convergence gives \[\operatorname{dist}(0,G_{\bar\varepsilon}(x_*))=\lim_{k\to\infty}\|g_k\|\le\bar\nu.\] Thus persistent positive sampling radius and tolerance yield only \((\bar\varepsilon,\bar\nu)\)-neighborhood stationarity. In particular, neither \(0\in\partial^C f(x_*)\) nor exact local optimality follows merely from this fixed-resolution conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a fixed positive radius, consistent sampled hulls can certify only that the limiting neighborhood-gradient hull lies within the positive residual tolerance of zero.

children.title: Vanishing-Radius Clarke Stationarity
children.top_down_role: Asymptotic Clarke-stationarity behavior under refined sampling resolution.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is locally Lipschitz near \(x_*\).
\(x_k\to x_*\), \(\varepsilon_k\downarrow0\), and \(g_k\in G_k\) satisfies \(\|g_k\|\to0\).
Every cluster limit of vectors \(v_k\in G_k\) belongs to \(\partial^C f(x_*)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Then \(0\in\partial^C f(x_*)\), so \(x_*\) is Clarke stationary.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic consistency statement underlying almost-sure gradient-sampling convergence.

source_refs.locator: 7.1 Nonsmooth Analysis I: Clarke's Calculus p. 626

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g_k\in G_k\) be sampled convex combinations with \(\|g_k\|\to0\). Then \(g_k\to0\). By sampling consistency, every cluster limit of such vectors belongs to \(\partial^C f(x_*)\). Hence \[0\in\partial^C f(x_*).\] Therefore any cluster point reached along a sequence whose sampling radii and sampled residuals both vanish is Clarke stationary. In a randomized implementation, this conclusion is almost sure only after establishing that the required sampling-consistency event has probability one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If iterates converge while sampling radii and consistent sampled residuals vanish, the limit contains zero in its Clarke subdifferential.

children.title: Positive-Tolerance Finite Termination
children.top_down_role: Termination theory under nonzero computational tolerances.

assumptions_latex: The initial level set is compact and \(f\) is locally Lipschitz on a neighborhood of it.
Accepted steps satisfy a uniform sufficient-decrease rule whenever \(\|g_k\|>\nu_k\).
The targets satisfy \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tar}}>0\) and \(\nu_{\mathrm{tar}}>0\), with finitely many contractions needed to reach them.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Under the stated consistency and decrease assumptions, the method reaches the positive-resolution termination test after finitely many iterations.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite termination at strictly positive computational resolutions, conditional on standard globalization hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose the algorithm contracts \(\varepsilon_k\) and \(
u_k\) geometrically after successful tests \(\|g_k\|\le
u_k\), and terminates when \(\varepsilon_k\le\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tar}}\) and \(\|g_k\|\le
u_{\mathrm{tar}}\). Assume that, at every fixed resolution above the targets, either the stationarity test is eventually met or accepted steps produce sufficient decrease incompatible with infinitely many iterations in the compact level set. Since only finitely many geometric contractions are required to reach each positive target, the method terminates after finitely many iterations. For random sampling, the assertion holds on the probability-one event on which all fixed-resolution consistency properties hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With compact level sets, reliable sampling, sufficient decrease, and positive target tolerances, geometric resolution refinement reaches the termination test in finitely many iterations.

children.title: Revised Gradient-Sampling Convergence
children.top_down_role: Strengthened convergence alternatives for revised gradient-sampling schemes.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is locally Lipschitz and bounded below on the initial level set.
A revised scheme produces monotone accepted values, vanishing resolutions, and sampling-consistent hulls.
Every infinite run has refinement indices \(k_j\) with \(\|g_{k_j}\|\to0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Max Local Rate Regime

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le q} f_i(x)\), where every \(f_i\) is twice continuously differentiable near a Clarke-stationary point \(x_*\). knowledge_statements.title: Incremental Sample Acquisition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adaptive enlargement of a gradient sample by small batches rather than complete resampling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x_k\in\mathbb R^n\), radius \(\epsilon_k>0\), an initial differentiability sample \(Y_k\subset B(x_k,\epsilon_k)\), and batch size \(b\ge1\), form \(G_k=\{\nabla f(y):y\in Y_k\}\). Solve the minimum-norm hull problem \(g_k\in\mathop{\rm argmin}_{g\in\operatorname{conv}G_k}\|g\|\). If the model-quality or stationarity test fails, draw at most \(b\) new differentiability points in \(B(x_k,\epsilon_k)\), append their gradients to \(G_k\), and resolve. Stop upon passing the test or reaching a prescribed sample cap; output \(g_k\) and the enlarged sample.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Build the sampled gradient hull gradually, adding small batches and resolving until a quality test passes or a sample limit is reached.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is locally Lipschitz and differentiable almost everywhere.
Sampled points are chosen where \(f\) is differentiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is a minimum-norm vector from the incrementally enlarged sampled-gradient hull.

gradients collected at the current iteration

children.title: Gradient-Sample Reuse

knowledge_statements.title: Gradient-Sample Reuse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Retention of previously evaluated gradients that remain geometrically valid for the new sampling neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: After moving from \(x_k\) to \(x_{k+1}\), retain every stored pair \((y,\nabla f(y))\) satisfying \(y\in B(x_{k+1},\epsilon_{k+1})\) and the algorithm's differentiability and freshness requirements. Discard all other pairs, sample additional differentiability points until the required hull size or adequacy test is attained, and define \(G_{k+1}\) from the retained and newly acquired gradients. Compute the next sampled direction from \(\operatorname{conv}G_{k+1}\). Reuse changes gradient-evaluation cost but not the defining neighborhood of the sampled model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Keep old gradients only when their evaluation points remain valid in the new sampling ball, then supplement them as needed.
assumptions_latex: Stored gradients retain their associated evaluation points.
The new radius \(\epsilon_{k+1}>0\) is known.

knowledge_statements.title: Hull-Subproblem Warm Starts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Warm-starting the minimum-norm convex-hull problem after incremental changes to the gradient sample.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For sampled gradients \(g_1,\\ldots,g_m\), write the hull subproblem as \(\min_{\lambda\in\Delta_m}\frac12\|G\lambda\|^2\), where \(G=[g_1\ \cdots\ g_m]\) and \(\Delta_m=\{\lambda\ge0:\mathbf1^T\lambda=1\}\). When gradients are retained, removed, or appended, restrict the preceding coefficient vector to retained columns, renormalize it when its mass is positive, assign zero coefficients to new columns, and use the resulting feasible vector to initialize the new solve. If no positive mass remains, initialize with any simplex vertex.

knowledge_statements.title: Quasi-Newton Gradient Sampling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gradient sampling in a uniformly safeguarded positive-definite quasi-Newton metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At iteration \(k\), sample differentiability points near \(x_k\), form the gradient matrix \(G_k\), and choose a symmetric metric \(H_k\) satisfying \(mI\preceq H_k\preceq MI\) for fixed \(0<m\le M<\infty\). Solve \(\min_{\lambda\in\Delta}\frac12(G_k\lambda)^T H_k(G_k\lambda)\), set \(g_k=G_k\lambda_k\) and \(d_k=-H_k g_k\), and globalize the step by the prescribed line search. After an accepted step, update \(H_k\) by a safeguarded quasi-Newton formula; skip, damp, or project any update that would violate the spectral bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compute the sampled minimum-norm combination in a bounded positive-definite quasi-Newton metric, then safeguard every metric update.

The line search and sampling-radius rules are specified.

knowledge_statements.title: Spectral Gradient Sampling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar variable-metric gradient sampling with safeguarded secant-based spectral scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Form a sampled aggregate gradient \(g_k\in\operatorname{conv}G_k\). For accepted consecutive iterates define \(s_{k-1}=x_k-x_{k-1}\) and \(y_{k-1}=g_k-g_{k-1}\). Otherwise use a prescribed safeguarded default scale. Apply the gradient-sampling line search to \(d_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scale the sampled aggregate gradient by a bounded Barzilai–Borwein-type scalar computed from consecutive steps and aggregate-gradient changes.

Aggregate gradients are computed consistently at consecutive accepted iterates.

children.title: Random-Perturbation Variants

knowledge_statements.title: Random-Perturbation Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Random displacement of exceptional points to obtain gradients at nearby differentiability points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x_k\), radius \(\epsilon_k>0\), and an absolutely continuous distribution supported on \(B(0,\epsilon_k)\), draw perturbations \(u_{k,j}\) and query \(f\) at \(y_{k,j}=x_k+u_{k,j}\). If a differentiability test or gradient evaluation fails, redraw according to the prescribed retry rule. For a locally Lipschitz objective, differentiability holds almost everywhere, so an absolutely continuous draw encounters the nondifferentiability set with probability zero. Use the successfully evaluated gradients to form the sampled hull and compute the gradient-sampling direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Draw nearby points from a continuous distribution; almost surely they are differentiability points of a locally Lipschitz objective, so their gradients can populate the sampled hull.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is locally Lipschitz near the sampling ball.
Each perturbation distribution is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure.

children.title: Nonmonotone Acceptance Variants

knowledge_statements.title: Nonmonotone Acceptance Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-memory sufficient-decrease tests permitting controlled objective increases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d_k\) be a sampled search direction, \(t_k>0\), \(c\in(0,1)\), and \(M\ge0\). Define \(R_k=\max\{f(x_{k-j}):0\le j\le\min(k,M)\}\). A trial point \(x_k+t_kd_k\) is accepted when \[f(x_k+t_kd_k)\le R_k+c t_k g_k^T d_k,\] where \(g_k\) is the sampled aggregate used to construct \(d_k\) and \(g_k^Td_k<0\). With \(M=0\), the condition reduces to the monotone Armijo test; positive \(M\) permits increases relative to \(f(x_k)\) while enforcing decrease relative to the reference window.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Accept a trial step if it gives Armijo decrease relative to the largest recent objective value, allowing controlled nonmonotonicity.
assumptions_latex: \(c\in(0,1)\) and \(M\) is a nonnegative integer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The accepted trial satisfies the finite-memory nonmonotone Armijo inequality.

notation.meaning: maximum objective value in the finite reference window

children.title: Null-Step Refinement Variants

knowledge_statements.title: Null-Step Refinement Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Model refinement after a rejected trial without changing the serious iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a rejected trial from \(x_k\), declare a null step and keep \(x_{k+1}=x_k\). Refine the sampled model by decreasing the radius, enlarging or replacing the gradient sample, or both, subject to the variant's prescribed rules. Recompute an aggregate gradient \(g_{k+1}\) from the refined hull and generate a new direction. Continue refinement until a trial satisfies the acceptance condition, a stationarity tolerance is met, or a specified safeguard terminates the inner loop. A null step updates model information but does not change the accepted iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After rejection, keep the iterate fixed, refine the sampling radius or gradient hull, and retry until acceptance, stationarity, or a safeguard occurs.
assumptions_latex: A trial step has failed the current acceptance test.
The refinement rule preserves a positive sampling radius until termination.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At every null step, \(x_{k+1}=x_k\) while the sampled model is refined.

notation.meaning: aggregate gradient of the refined sampled hull

knowledge_statements.title: Inadequate-Sample Recovery Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recovery when the current gradient sample cannot support a reliable direction or stationarity decision.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Declare the current sample inadequate when its size, geometry, numerical conditioning, or model-consistency test fails the prescribed threshold. Do not certify stationarity from that hull. Keep the current accepted iterate, obtain additional or replacement gradients at differentiability points in the current sampling ball, and recompute the minimum-norm hull vector. If adequacy remains unattainable, apply the variant's safeguarded radius adjustment or terminate with an explicit sampling-failure status. Resume the ordinary acceptance procedure only after the adequacy predicate holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the sample is too small, ill-conditioned, or inconsistent, withhold stationarity, resample at the same iterate, and resume only after adequacy is restored.
assumptions_latex: The algorithm supplies an explicit, computable sample-adequacy predicate.
Failed gradient evaluations are distinguishable from valid evaluations.

knowledge_statements.title: Derivative-Free Sampling Extensions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A generic value-based gradient-sampling extension using consistent local interpolation models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At \(x_k\in\mathbb R^n\), choose sample centers \(y_{k,j}\in B(x_k,\varepsilon_k)\). Around each center, evaluate \(f\) at a poised interpolation set of diameter at most \(h_k\), construct an affine model \(m_{k,j}(z)=a_{k,j}+g_{k,j}^{\mathsf T}(z-y_{k,j})\), and compute
\[\bar g_k=\operatorname*{argmin}_{g\in\operatorname{conv}\{g_{k,1},\ldots,g_{k,m}\}}\|g\|.\]
If \(\|\bar g_k\|\leq\nu_k\), reduce \(\varepsilon_k,h_k,\nu_k\), or terminate at final tolerances. Otherwise apply a value-based sufficient-decrease test along \(d_k=-\bar g_k\) and set \(x_{k+1}=x_k+t_kd_k\).

The interpolation sets are uniformly poised.
The model gradients are consistent as \(h_k\downarrow0\) at differentiability points.

children.title: Directionally Lipschitz Extension Boundary
children.top_down_role: The horizon-geometry boundary beyond standard locally Lipschitz theory.

knowledge_statements.title: Directionally Lipschitz Extension Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The horizon-subdifferential boundary separating compact locally Lipschitz geometry from directional extensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a proper lower-semicontinuous function \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) finite at \(\bar x\), local Lipschitz continuity entails
\[\partial^\infty f(\bar x)=\{0\}.\]
Thus ordinary gradient sampling operates with bounded local generalized-gradient geometry. A directionally Lipschitz extension may admit \(\partial^\infty f(\bar x)\neq\{0\}\), but requires the relevant horizon cone to be pointed, namely
\[\partial^\infty f(\bar x)\cap\bigl(-\partial^\infty f(\bar x)\bigr)=\{0\}.\]
When this pointedness fails, the horizon geometry contains a line; normalization or specialized directional constructions are then required, and the compact minimum-norm sampled-hull model is not directly applicable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonzero horizon subgradients mark departure from local Lipschitzness. Pointed horizon geometry permits directional extensions; a horizon line defeats the usual compact sampled-gradient hull model.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and finite at \(\bar x\).
Horizon subdifferentials are interpreted in the finite-dimensional limiting sense.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The standard compact-hull regime has \(\partial^\infty f(\bar x)=\{0\}\); directional extension requires at least pointed horizon geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: General Non-Lipschitz Failure Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A one-dimensional example showing loss of bounded sampled-gradient geometry without local Lipschitz continuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) defined by \(f(x)=|x|^{1/2}\). It is continuous but not locally Lipschitz at \(0\), and for \(x\neq0\),
\[f'(x)=\frac{\operatorname{sign}(x)}{2\sqrt{|x|}}.\]
Hence every sequence \(x_j\to0\) with \(x_j\neq0\) satisfies \(|f'(x_j)|\to\infty\). Consequently, sampled gradients in shrinking neighborhoods of \(0\) are not uniformly bounded and their convex hulls need not converge to a compact generalized-gradient set. The usual Clarke-gradient-sampling interpretation therefore fails at \(0\), even though function values remain finite and continuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the square-root cusp, nearby derivatives diverge. Shrinking-neighborhood gradient samples therefore cannot approximate a bounded Clarke subdifferential at the origin.
assumptions_latex: Sampling points are nonzero and approach \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup\{|f'(x)|:0<|x|<\varepsilon\}=+\infty\) for every \(\varepsilon>0\), so bounded sampled-gradient hull geometry fails.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), and suppose that there exists \(\rho>0\) such that \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is locally Lipschitz on an open set containing \(\overline B(x,\rho)\). For \(0<\varepsilon<\rho\), define
\[\partial^C_\varepsilon f(x)=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}\!\bigcup_{y\in\overline B(x,\varepsilon)}\partial^C f(y).\]
Each set \(\partial^C_\varepsilon f(x)\) is nonempty, compact, and convex. Moreover, if \(0<\varepsilon_1\leq\varepsilon_2<\rho\), then \(\partial^C_{\varepsilon_1}f(x)\subseteq\partial^C_{\varepsilon_2}f(x)\), and
\[\partial^C f(x)=\bigcap_{0<\varepsilon<\rho}\partial^C_\varepsilon f(x).\]
Thus these sets form nested outer approximations of the Clarke subdifferential as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Close and convexify all Clarke subgradients on a sufficiently small closed neighborhood of the center. These nonempty compact convex outer approximations are nested and shrink to the Clarke subdifferential at the center.

knowledge_statements.title: Discrete-Gradient Subgradient Approximations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-difference vectors satisfying a discrete mean-value identity along sampled displacements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x,y\in\mathbb R^n\) with \(x\neq y\), a discrete gradient of \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) over \((x,y)\) is any computable vector \(g_D(x,y)\in\mathbb R^n\), obtained from finitely many function evaluations, satisfying
\[f(y)-f(x)=\langle g_D(x,y),y-x\rangle.\]
A finite-radius subgradient approximation at \(x\) is then
\[G_D(x;\varepsilon)=\operatorname{conv}\{g_D(x,y_j):0<\|y_j-x\|\leq\varepsilon,\ j=1,\ldots,m\}.\]
It is an approximate, sampling-dependent object; membership of its elements in \(\partial^C f(x)\) is not asserted without an additional consistency theorem for the chosen discrete-gradient construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A discrete gradient uses finitely many values and reproduces a sampled function difference. Convex hulls of such vectors provide method-dependent approximate subgradient information.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is finite at all evaluation points.
The discrete-gradient rule uses finitely many function values and satisfies the displayed identity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G_D(x;\varepsilon)\) is a finite convex approximation whose generalized-subgradient validity requires scheme-specific consistency assumptions.

knowledge_statements.title: Sampled-Subgradient Approximations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite convex hulls of generalized gradients sampled in a neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be locally Lipschitz near \(x\), choose \(y_1,\ldots,y_m\in B(x,\varepsilon)\), and select \(v_j\in\partial^C f(y_j)\). The sampled-subgradient approximation is
\[G_m(x;\varepsilon)=\operatorname{conv}\{v_1,\ldots,v_m\}.\]
It always satisfies \(G_m(x;\varepsilon)\subseteq\partial^C_\varepsilon f(x)\). If successive samples become graph-dense in \(\{(y,v):y\in B(x,\varepsilon),\ v\in\partial^C f(y)\}\), then the compact hulls converge in Hausdorff distance to \(\partial^C_\varepsilon f(x)\). Sending \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\) subsequently recovers the local Clarke geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convexify finitely many nearby Clarke subgradients. Graph-dense sampling fills the continuous epsilon-enlargement, which shrinks to the local Clarke subdifferential.

knowledge_statements.title: Limited-Memory Discrete-Gradient Bundle Method
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A bundle-discrete-gradient iteration retaining at most a fixed number of recent or active vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix a memory limit \(M\geq1\). At iteration \(k\), compute new discrete gradients \(G_k^{\mathrm{new}}\), combine them with a retained bundle \(B_{k-1}\), and select \(B_k\subseteq B_{k-1}\cup G_k^{\mathrm{new}}\) with \(|B_k|\leq M\), retaining the newest vectors and any vectors active in the preceding aggregation. Compute
\[\bar g_k=\operatorname*{argmin}_{g\in\operatorname{conv}B_k}\|g\|.\]
If \(\|\bar g_k\|\) is below tolerance, reduce the sampling radius or stop. Otherwise use \(-\bar g_k\) in a sufficient-decrease line search, update the iterate, and discard nonretained bundle elements before the next iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Retain a bounded bundle of new and active discrete gradients, aggregate it by minimum norm, and use the result for descent or stationarity testing.
assumptions_latex: The memory limit satisfies \(M\geq1\).
Every retained vector is a discrete gradient generated at a recorded nearby point.
The line search uses actual function values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At every iteration \(|B_k|\leq M\), so aggregation storage remains bounded independently of \(k\).

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Norm Discrete-Gradient Aggregation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A projection certificate for sampled stationarity and common descent across a finite discrete-gradient hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a nonempty finite set \(G=\{g_1,\ldots,g_m\}\subset\mathbb R^n\), let
\[\bar g=\operatorname*{argmin}_{g\in\operatorname{conv}G}\|g\|.\]
The projection optimality condition is
\[\langle g-\bar g,\bar g\rangle\geq0\qquad\text{for every }g\in\operatorname{conv}G.\]
Consequently, if \(\bar g\neq0\), then \(d=-\bar g\) satisfies \(\langle g,d\rangle\leq-\|\bar g\|^2\) for every \(g\in G\), certifying common strict descent for the sampled linear models. If \(\|\bar g\|\leq\eta\), then \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\operatorname{conv}G)\leq\eta\), certifying \(\eta\)-stationarity relative to the sampled hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The projection of zero onto the sampled hull either yields a common descent direction or certifies that the hull lies within the chosen stationarity tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(G\subset\mathbb R^n\) is finite and nonempty.
Stationarity is interpreted relative to \(\operatorname{conv}G\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Either \(-\bar g\) is common descent for all sampled linear models, or \(\|\bar g\|\leq\eta\) certifies sampled-hull \(\eta\)-stationarity.

knowledge_statements.title: Component-Dependency Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An incidence representation of partially separable objectives and their active variable blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A component-dependency representation of \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is
\[f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^q f_i(P_i x),\]
where \(J_i\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) is the variable set used by component \(f_i\), and \(P_i:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^{|J_i|}\) extracts those coordinates. Equivalently, the binary incidence matrix \(A\in\{0,1\}^{q\times n}\) is defined by \(A_{ij}=1\) exactly when \(j\in J_i\). A perturbation supported on coordinates \(S\) can change only components with \(J_i\cap S\neq\varnothing\), permitting evaluations to be localized to the corresponding incidence neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Represent the objective as a sum of components, each depending on a coordinate subset. The incidence matrix identifies exactly which component values a perturbation can change.
assumptions_latex: \(f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^q f_i(P_i x)\) for specified coordinate projections \(P_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A perturbation on \(S\) leaves every component with \(J_i\cap S=\varnothing\) unchanged.

knowledge_statements.title: Componentwise Discrete-Gradient Computation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Construction and sparse embedding of discrete gradients for partially separable objective components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose \(f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^q f_i(P_i x)\). For a displacement \(s\in\mathbb R^n\), compute for every affected component a vector \(g_i\in\mathbb R^{|J_i|}\) from finitely many component evaluations such that
\[f_i(P_i(x+s))-f_i(P_i x)=\langle g_i,P_i s\rangle.\]
Set the aggregate discrete gradient to
\[g_D(x,x+s)=\sum_{i=1}^q P_i^{\mathsf T}g_i.\]
Then \(f(x+s)-f(x)=\langle g_D(x,x+s),s\rangle\). Components with \(P_i s=0\) require no reevaluation and may contribute any stored vector whose inner product with \(P_i s\) is zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compute discrete gradients only for components affected by a displacement, embed them into the full space, and sum them to preserve the discrete mean-value identity.

where the ordered sets \(S_1,\ldots,S_m\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) satisfy \(S_i\cap S_j=\varnothing\) for \(|i-j|>1\). For coordinate \(j\), define \(I(j)=\{i:j\in S_i\}\). Then
\[
f(x+h e_j)-f(x)=\sum_{i\in I(j)}\bigl(\phi_i((x+h e_j)_{S_i})-\phi_i(x_{S_i})\bigr).
\]
Thus only the components in \(I(j)\) enter that sampled difference; when \(d=\max_j|I(j)|\) is small, cached component values reduce per-coordinate reevaluation from \(m\) components to at most \(d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A chained model sums locally dependent components whose nonneighboring dependency sets do not overlap. A coordinate perturbation changes only its incident components, allowing cached values to reduce reevaluation cost.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic value-oracle accounting for one discrete-gradient construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a deterministic discrete-gradient routine querying a value oracle at points \(x^{(0)},\ldots,x^{(q-1)}\in\mathbb{R}^n\), its function-evaluation complexity is
\[
Q_f=\left|\{x^{(0)},\ldots,x^{(q-1)}\}\right|.
\]
A cached repeated query is not counted again. If \(f=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\phi_i\) and the oracle exposes the individual \(\phi_i\), define the component cost by
\[
Q_{\mathrm{comp}}=\sum_{i=1}^{m}N_i,
\]
where \(N_i\) is the number of distinct arguments at which \(\phi_i\) is evaluated. Claims involving \(Q_{\mathrm{comp}}\) require such a decomposed oracle and do not follow from black-box access to \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Evaluation complexity counts distinct value-oracle sample points. Component-level accounting is a different model and is valid only when the objective decomposition is directly accessible.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Naive forward coordinate sampling with a common base point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(h\ne0\). The forward coordinate-sampling vector
\[
g_j(x;h)=\frac{f(x+h e_j)-f(x)}{h},\qquad j=1,\ldots,n,
\]
uses the sample set \(\{x,x+h e_1,\ldots,x+h e_n\}\). These points are distinct, so one complete construction requires exactly
\[
Q_f=n+1
\]
value-oracle evaluations when no values were previously cached. Consequently \(Q_f\in\Theta(n)\). This count concerns sampling cost only; it does not assert that the vector is a classical gradient or a valid generalized subgradient at a nonsmooth point.

assumptions_latex: The objective is \(f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\phi_i(x_{S_i})\), and each component oracle is accessible.
The unperturbed component values are cached.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Component-oracle cost under known additive dependency structure and caching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\phi_i(x_{S_i})\), let \(I(j)=\{i:j\in S_i\}\) and \(D=\sum_{j=1}^{n}|I(j)|\). Evaluate and cache all \(m\) components at \(x\). For each coordinate perturbation \(x+h e_j\), reevaluate only components in \(I(j)\). Then a complete coordinate sweep has component-evaluation cost
\[
Q_{\mathrm{comp}}\le m+D.
\]
If \(|I(j)|\le d\) for every \(j\), then \(Q_{\mathrm{comp}}\le m+nd\). Thus bounded incidence gives \(Q_{\mathrm{comp}}\in O(m+nd)\), whereas reevaluating every component at every sample costs \(m(n+1)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With exposed components and cached base values, coordinate sampling costs m plus the total dependency incidences. Bounded incidence replaces repeated dense component evaluation by structure-adjusted work.

children.title: Noise-Sensitive Difference Approximations
children.top_down_role: Reliability loss caused by noisy or numerically unstable function differences.

assumptions_latex: Observed values satisfy \(\widetilde f(z)=f(z)+\eta(z)\) with \(|\eta(z)|\le\delta\).
The forward difference uses a nonzero step \(h\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The noise contribution to each difference quotient is bounded by \(2\delta/|h|\), so decreasing the step amplifies worst-case evaluation noise.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic bounded additive noise in forward function differences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\widetilde f(z)=f(z)+\eta(z)\) with \(|\eta(z)|\le\delta\) for every queried \(z\). For \(h\ne0\), define
\[
\widetilde g_j=\frac{\widetilde f(x+h e_j)-\widetilde f(x)}{h},\qquad g_j=\frac{f(x+h e_j)-f(x)}{h}.
\]
Then
\[
|\widetilde g_j-g_j|=\frac{|\eta(x+h e_j)-\eta(x)|}{|h|}\le\frac{2\delta}{|h|}.
\]
Hence no uniform reliability guarantee based solely on bounded value noise can improve as \(|h|\to0\); absent additional noise structure, the worst-case difference error diverges like \(1/|h|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bounded value errors of size delta can create difference-quotient errors as large as 2 delta divided by the step. Very small steps therefore amplify noise.
knowledge_statements.title: Noise-Sensitive Difference Approximations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bounded-noise estimate is mathematically correct and the failure-boundary kind fits, but no numerical-differentiation or discrete-gradient source with a locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Forward, Central, and Backward Finite-Difference Derivative Approximations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional first-derivative quotients and their finite-precision failure boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a function \(f\), point \(x\), and nonzero step \(h\), the forward, centered, and backward difference quotients are \[\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h},\qquad \frac{f(x+h/2)-f(x-h/2)}{h},\qquad \frac{f(x)-f(x-h)}{h}.\] If \(f\) is differentiable at \(x\), each converges to \(f'(x)\) as \(h\to0\) in exact arithmetic. In floating-point arithmetic, excessively small \(|h|\) can produce subtractive-cancellation error.

knowledge_statements.title: Dependency-Structure Mismatch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure caused by underestimating component-coordinate incidence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose \(f(x)=\sum_i\phi_i(x_{S_i})\), but an implementation uses declared sets \(\widehat S_i\) and, after perturbing coordinate \(j\), reevaluates only \(\widehat I(j)=\{i:j\in\widehat S_i\}\). Let \(I(j)=\{i:j\in S_i\}\) and \(E(j)=I(j)\setminus\widehat I(j)\). The discrepancy between the true objective difference and the cached calculation is
\[
\sum_{i\in E(j)}\bigl(\phi_i((x+h e_j)_{S_i})-\phi_i(x_{S_i})\bigr).
\]
Therefore the cached difference is incorrect whenever this total omitted change is nonzero. The containment condition \(S_i\subseteq\widehat S_i\) for every \(i\) is sufficient for exact reuse; overestimating dependencies preserves correctness but may reduce savings.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Omitted component-coordinate dependencies make the cached difference incorrect whenever their total omitted change is nonzero. Declared dependency sets containing all true sets guarantee correctness, while extra dependencies only increase cost.
assumptions_latex: The objective is \(f(x)=\sum_i\phi_i(x_{S_i})\).
The implementation uses declared dependency sets \(\widehat S_i\) to select components for reevaluation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An underestimated dependency structure can produce an incorrect sampled difference; the condition \(S_i\subseteq\widehat S_i\) for every \(i\) is sufficient for exact structural reuse.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case all-to-all component-coordinate dependence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\phi_i(x)\) with every \(\phi_i\) depending nontrivially on every coordinate. Then \(I(j)=\{1,\ldots,m\}\) for each \(j\), and
\[
D=\sum_{j=1}^{n}|I(j)|=mn.
\]
The cached structure-aware sweep therefore has
\[
Q_{\mathrm{comp}}=m+D=m(n+1),
\]
provided every incident component must be reevaluated. This equals the component count obtained by evaluating all \(m\) components at the base point and at each of the \(n\) coordinate perturbations; dependency sparsity provides no reduction in this dense regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When every component depends on every coordinate, the incidence count is mn. Structure-aware sampling then costs m(n+1), exactly the dense component-evaluation count.

assumptions_latex: A coordinate sweep uses cached component values and a declared incidence relation.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Linear-in-dimension savings require bounded or sublinear incidence; if \(d_n\) grows proportionally to the component count, the sparse bound becomes dense-order.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic boundary between sparse-incidence and dense-incidence cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a family indexed by \(n\), let \(m_n\) be the component count and \(d_n=\max_j|I(j)|\). The cached incidence bound is
\[
Q_{\mathrm{comp}}\le m_n+n d_n.
\]
If \(d_n\in O(1)\), this is \(O(m_n+n)\). If instead \(d_n\in\Theta(m_n)\) and a fixed positive fraction of coordinates has \(\Theta(m_n)\) incident components, then
\[
Q_{\mathrm{comp}}\in\Theta(m_n n),
\]
up to the base evaluations. Thus sparsity savings disappear when typical coordinate incidence grows at the same order as the total component count.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bounded coordinate incidence yields sparse linear-style cost. If a positive fraction of coordinates touches order m components, the component cost returns to dense order mn.

assumptions_latex: The objective class consists of proper functions \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\).

notation.meaning: feasible region on which regularity is imposed

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regularity axis for nonsmooth stationarity-oracle complexity statements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(L\ge0\). A Lipschitz function-class regime is specified by
\[
\mathcal F_L(X)=\{f: |f(x)-f(y)|\le L\|x-y\|\text{ for all }x,y\in X\}.
\]
An oracle-complexity statement must additionally identify the generalized subdifferential \(\partial f\) used in the stationarity criterion, for example
\[
\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x))\le\varepsilon.
\]
Changing local to global Lipschitz regularity, changing \(X\), or changing the subdifferential changes the admissible class and can change the attainable complexity; these choices are therefore part of the formal problem specification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stationarity complexity regime must specify where and with what modulus functions are Lipschitz, and which generalized subdifferential defines epsilon-stationarity.
knowledge_statements.title: Function-Class Regularity

children.title: Structural Problem Regimes

assumptions_latex: Each problem instance specifies an objective, feasible set, oracle, and stationarity measure.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Complexity comparisons across structural regimes are meaningful only when the oracle and stationarity conventions remain fixed and the structural predicates are stated explicitly.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formal comparability requirement for structured nonsmooth oracle bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A structural oracle-complexity regime is a subclass
\[
\mathcal P_{\mathsf S}=\{P\in\mathcal P:P\text{ satisfies the predicate }\mathsf S\},
\]
where \(\mathsf S\) may encode convexity, weak convexity, finite-sum form, composite form, or dependency sparsity. For a fixed oracle model and residual, define
\[
T_{\mathsf S}(\varepsilon)=\inf_A\sup_{P\in\mathcal P_{\mathsf S}}N_{\mathcal O_P}\bigl(A,P,\varepsilon\bigr),
\]
where successful output means \(r_P(x)\le\varepsilon\). Bounds for two structural predicates are directly comparable only if they use the same oracle information, success criterion, and deterministic or randomized convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A structural regime is a precisely defined subclass of problems. Its oracle complexity is comparable with another regime only under identical oracle, stationarity, and success conventions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower-boundedness condition supporting initial-gap oracle bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The globally lower-bounded regime consists of proper objectives satisfying
\[
f_{\inf}:=\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}f(x)>-\infty.
\]
For an initial point \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f\), define
\[
\Delta_0=f(x_0)-f_{\inf}\in[0,+\infty).
\]

children.title: Finite-Time Exact-Stationarity Impossibility

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Time Exact-Stationarity Impossibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Broad black-box locally Lipschitz classes under finite local first-order information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a deterministic algorithm that makes finitely many adaptive queries to a local oracle for an unknown locally Lipschitz function and then outputs \(x_A\). Exact Clarke stationarity cannot be guaranteed whenever the function class has the following adversarial-completion property: every finite oracle transcript consistent with one member admits another transcript-consistent member \(\widetilde f\) satisfying \(0\notin\partial_C\widetilde f(x_A)\). Under this property, no finite query bound certifies \(0\in\partial_C f(x_A)\) uniformly over the class; additional structure, nonlocal information, approximation, or randomization with a weaker success criterion is necessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If every finite local transcript has a consistent completion nonstationary at the output, no deterministic finite-query method guarantees exact Clarke stationarity.
assumptions_latex: The algorithm receives only finitely many responses from a local oracle.
The function class has the stated adversarial-completion property.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_{\mathrm{search}}(\varepsilon=0)=+\infty\)

knowledge_statements.title: Single-Point Small-Subgradient Impossibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of finite local information to certify a small subgradient at the reported point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(\varepsilon>0\). Suppose that, after every finite transcript of a local-oracle algorithm with reported point \(x_A\), there exists a transcript-consistent function \(\widetilde f\) in the admissible locally Lipschitz class such that \[\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial_C\widetilde f(x_A))>\varepsilon.\] Then the transcript cannot certify the single-point condition \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial_C f(x_A))\leq\varepsilon\), and no finite-query algorithm has a uniform guarantee of that form. This obstruction does not by itself exclude neighborhood stationarity based on convex combinations of subgradients sampled near \(x_A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite transcript cannot certify a small subgradient at its output if a consistent function has residual greater than the requested tolerance there.
assumptions_latex: \(\varepsilon>0\).
The oracle is local and the class admits the stated transcript-consistent completion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{f\text{ consistent}}\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial_C f(x_A))>\varepsilon\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conditional obstruction is logically coherent and correctly distinguishes single-point from neighborhood stationarity, but its applicable oracle and function-class range cannot be assessed without an authoritative lower-bound source.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transcript equivalence as a general mechanism for deterministic oracle lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) be a deterministic adaptive algorithm making at most \(T\in\mathbb{N}_0\) local-oracle queries. Two instances \(f_0\) and \(f_1\) are indistinguishable to \(A\) through time \(T\) when their oracle responses agree recursively at every point queried by \(A\). The algorithm then generates the same transcript and the same output \(x_T\) on both instances. Consequently, for a required output predicate \(P(f,x)\), if \[\neg\exists x\;\bigl(P(f_0,x)\wedge P(f_1,x)\bigr),\] then the common output cannot be valid for both instances, and \(A\) fails on at least one of them.

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Momentum First-Order Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic neighborhood-sampling momentum scheme; no oracle-complexity guarantee is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a locally Lipschitz function \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\), initialize \(x_0\in\mathbb R^d\) and \(m_0=0\). At iteration \(k\), sample \(u_k\) from the ball \(\delta\mathbb B\), query \(g_k=\nabla f(x_k+u_k)\) at a differentiability point, and set \(m_{k+1}=(1-\beta_k)m_k+\beta_k g_k\). If \(\|m_{k+1}\|>\varepsilon\), update \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\eta_k m_{k+1}/\|m_{k+1}\|\); otherwise stop and output \(x_k\). A capped run outputs an iterate selected by its prescribed randomized or minimum-residual rule.

\(0<\beta_k\leq 1\), \(\eta_k>0\), and \(\delta,\varepsilon>0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Practical Random-Conic-Perturbation Methods

Stop with output \(x_k\) when \(\|a_k\|\leq\varepsilon\); otherwise set \(x_{k+1}=x_k-eta_k a_k/\|a_k\|\), possibly after a value-based acceptance test.

knowledge_statements.title: Randomized Zeroth-Order Goldstein Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-point randomized smoothing template using function values only.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a locally Lipschitz \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\), choose \(h\leq\delta\), batch size \(m\), and sample independent \(u_{k,i}\) uniformly from the unit sphere. Form \(z_{k,i}=\frac{d}{2h}\bigl(f(x_k+hu_{k,i})-f(x_k-hu_{k,i})\bigr)u_{k,i}\) and \(z_k=m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m z_{k,i}\). Stop when \(\|z_k\|\leq\varepsilon\); otherwise update \(x_{k+1}=x_k-eta_k z_k/\max\{\|z_k\|,tau\}\). Output the stopped point or a prespecified randomized iterate after the query budget expires.

assumptions_latex: \(f\) is locally Lipschitz on all queried neighborhoods.
\(0<h\leq\delta\), \(m\geq1\), and \(\tau>0\).
Function values can be queried exactly or with controlled noise.

knowledge_statements.title: General Lipschitz NAS Impossibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local-oracle impossibility for recovering genuine nearby Clarke-stationary witnesses without additional structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a finite-query local oracle and tolerances \(\delta>0\) and \(0<\varepsilon<L\). Over unrestricted \(L\)-Lipschitz nonconvex functions, oracle consistency permits two objectives agreeing on every queried neighborhood but having incompatible sets of points \(y\) satisfying \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial^{\mathrm C}f(y))\leq\varepsilon\). Consequently, no deterministic finite-query rule can universally recover a witness \(y\) with \(\|y-x\|\leq\delta\) and the stated Clarke residual from local information alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without structural assumptions, finitely many local queries cannot universally recover a nearby point with small Clarke-subgradient residual.

The oracle reveals information only locally at queried points.
The algorithm is deterministic and makes finitely many queries.

knowledge_statements.title: Dimension-Free NAS Lower-Bound Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formal criterion excluding query bounds independent of ambient dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q_{mathcal O}(d,delta,varepsilon;L,Delta)\) denote minimax queries needed to output \(x\) together with a witness \(y\) satisfying \(\|x-y\|\leq\delta\) and \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial^{\mathrm C}f(y))\leq\varepsilon\). A dimension-free NAS lower-bound regime holds when, for every finite budget \(q\), some dimension \(d\) and admissible \(L\)-Lipschitz objective force every \(q\)-query algorithm to fail with probability exceeding the permitted level. Hence \(\sup_d Q_{\mathcal O}(d,delta,varepsilon;L,Delta)=+infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: No query budget depending only on accuracy and Lipschitz data can solve nearby-witness stationarity uniformly over dimension.
assumptions_latex: The accuracy parameters and Lipschitz data are fixed independently of \(d\).
Success requires an explicit nearby witness, not merely an existential certificate.

children.title: Incremental Sample Insertion
children.top_down_role: Augmentation of a maintained hull with newly acquired samples.

knowledge_statements.title: Incremental Sample Insertion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Insertion of one sampled gradient into a maintained minimum-norm hull problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given stored points \(G_k=\{g_1,\ldots,g_k\}\subset\mathbb R^n\), a new point \(g_{k+1}\), and feasible weights \(\lambda^k\in\Delta_k\), form \(G_{k+1}=G_k\cup\{g_{k+1}\}\). Initialize \(\widehat\lambda=(\lambda^k,0)\in\Delta_{k+1}\), then solve or reoptimize \[\min_{\lambda\in\Delta_{k+1}}\left\|\sum_{i=1}^{k+1}\lambda_i g_i\right\|^2.\] Return an optimizer \(\lambda^{k+1}\), the hull point \(v_{k+1}=\sum_i\lambda_i^{k+1}g_i\), and its positive support. Stop the reoptimization when its chosen primal-dual residual tolerance is met.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Append the new sample with zero weight, reoptimize the simplex quadratic program, and return the new minimum-norm hull certificate.
assumptions_latex: \(G_k\) and \(g_{k+1}\) are finite vectors in \(\mathbb R^n\).
\(\lambda^k\in\Delta_k\) is a feasible stored weight vector.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v_{k+1}\) is the computed minimum-norm point of \(\operatorname{conv}(G_{k+1})\) to the prescribed solver tolerance.

notation.meaning: simplex of nonnegative weights summing to one
