children.title: Hull Warm Starts
children.top_down_role: Reuse of the previous hull solution after sample insertion.

knowledge_statements.title: Hull Warm Starts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible initialization after a sampled hull changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an old simplex vector \(\lambda\in\Delta_m\), construct a feasible start for the modified hull as follows. After insertion, append zero weights. After deleting indices \(D\), retain the weights on \(R=\{1,\ldots,m\}\setminus D\) and, when \(s=\sum_{i\in R}\lambda_i>0\), set \(\widehat\lambda_i=\lambda_i/s\). If \(s=0\), choose any retained vertex weight. Supply \(\widehat\lambda\), the retained active set, and available dual multipliers to the hull solver; terminate only after the solver reestablishes its prescribed optimality residuals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Embed or renormalize the previous weights to obtain a feasible initialization for the changed hull, then restore optimality numerically.
assumptions_latex: The modified hull retains at least one point.
The previous weights belong to the old simplex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat\lambda\) is feasible for the modified simplex and initializes subsequent hull reoptimization.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: simplex feasibility is preserved by zero extension or positive-mass renormalization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The primal feasibility constructions are standard and correctly stated, and algorithm is the proper content kind. A source is still required for the combined insertion/deletion warm-start mechanism, especially the unspecified transfer of dual multipliers and the solver-dependent termination interface.

children.title: Active-Support Reoptimization
children.top_down_role: Adjustment of the active hull support after incremental changes.

knowledge_statements.title: Active-Support Reoptimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Restricted hull optimization followed by support correction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(G=\{g_1,\ldots,g_m\}\subset\mathbb R^n\), a nonempty working support \(I\), and tolerance \(\tau\ge0\), solve the minimum-norm hull problem restricted to \(I\). Let \(v=\sum_{i\in I}\lambda_i g_i\). If every excluded index satisfies \(g_j^{\mathsf T}v\ge\|v\|^2-\tau\), return \((v,\lambda,I)\). Otherwise insert an index minimizing \(g_j^{\mathsf T}v-\|v\|^2\), reoptimize, and delete zero-weight indices. Repeat until the test holds or the prescribed iteration limit is reached.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimize on a working support, add a point violating hull optimality, remove zero weights, and repeat until certified.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite and nonempty.
\(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\) is initially nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At successful termination, \(v\) satisfies the finite-hull first-order optimality inequalities within tolerance \(\tau\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: displayed inequality is the projection optimality condition for the convex hull

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed excluded-point inequality is the correct finite-hull projection optimality test, and the content kind fits. No source supports this particular active-support algorithm, its tolerance convention, or its convergence behavior. The returned status when the iteration limit is reached is also unspecified.

children.title: Stale-Sample Removal
children.top_down_role: Removal of samples outside the operative neighborhood model.

knowledge_statements.title: Stale-Sample Removal
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Radius-based deletion from a local sampled-gradient model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the current query be \(x_k\in\mathbb R^n\), let stored samples be pairs \((y_i,g_i)\), and choose an operative radius \(r_k>0\). Define the retained set \(R_k=\{i:\|y_i-x_k\|\le r_k\}\). Delete every pair indexed outside \(R_k\); if \(R_k\) is empty, acquire a new sample before forming a hull. Restrict any stored weights to \(R_k\), renormalize them when their retained mass is positive, and reoptimize the minimum-norm hull. Output only samples lying in the declared neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Discard samples outside the current neighborhood, repair the simplex weights, and reoptimize the retained local hull.
assumptions_latex: Each stored gradient \(g_i\) is associated with its sampling point \(y_i\).
The operative radius \(r_k\) is positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every output sample satisfies \(\|y_i-x_k\|\le r_k\), and the returned weights are feasible for the retained hull.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: locality filtering directly enforces the declared neighborhood model

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The radius filter matches the leaf and the feasibility repair is mathematically reasonable, but this is a method-specific sample-management policy with no citation. The output behavior after an empty retained set and failed sample acquisition also needs a sourced specification.

children.title: Redundant-Sample Compression
children.top_down_role: Reduction of superfluous hull points while retaining operative geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Redundant-Sample Compression
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Support reduction preserving a selected sampled-hull certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given samples \(G=\{g_1,\ldots,g_m\}\subset\mathbb R^n\) and a certificate \(v=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i g_i\) with \(\lambda\in\Delta_m\), repeatedly find a nonzero vector \(a\) supported on the positive weights such that \(\sum_i a_i g_i=0\) and \(\sum_i a_i=0\). Choose a maximal feasible step \(t\) for which \(\lambda-ta\ge0\), replace \(\lambda\) by \(\lambda-ta\), and remove newly zero weights. Stop when no affine dependence remains; return the unchanged point \(v\) with at most \(\operatorname{affdim}(G)+1\) positive weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Eliminate affine dependencies among positive-weight samples while preserving the represented hull point and simplex feasibility.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite in \(\mathbb R^n\).
\(v\) has the supplied convex representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned weights represent the same \(v\) and have support size at most \(\operatorname{affdim}(G)+1\).

children.title: Sampling-Set Adequacy Tests
children.top_down_role: Diagnostics for local directional and geometric coverage.

knowledge_statements.title: Sampling-Set Adequacy Tests
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric directional-coverage diagnostic for a local sampling set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a query \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) and distinct sampling points \(y_i\), set \(u_i=(y_i-x)/\|y_i-x\|\) and \[\sigma(U)=\min_{\|d\|=1}\max_i d^{\mathsf T}u_i.\] Given thresholds \(r>0\) and \(\eta>0\), certify geometric sampling adequacy when \(0<\|y_i-x\|\le r\) for every \(i\) and \(\sigma(U)\ge\eta\). The second inequality is equivalent to the normalized directions positively spanning \(\mathbb R^n\) with margin at least \(\eta\); the certificate diagnoses directional coverage but does not alone certify subdifferential accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Samples are geometrically adequate when they lie locally and their normalized displacements positively span every direction with a prescribed margin.
assumptions_latex: The query and sampling points lie in \(\mathbb R^n\).
No sampling point used in the test equals the query.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma(U)\ge\eta>0\) certifies quantitative directional coverage of \(\mathbb R^n\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: positive-spanning margin is a checkable finite-dimensional coverage diagnostic

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The positive-spanning margin is a coherent finite-dimensional geometric certificate and the statement correctly limits its implication. No source is supplied for adopting this particular margin and threshold pair as the sampling-adequacy interface in this taxonomy.

children.title: Nonsmooth Stationarity Stopping Tests
children.top_down_role: Stopping interfaces based on sampled certificates and neighborhood resolution.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonsmooth Stationarity Stopping Tests
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-tolerance stopping certificate using locality and a sampled gradient hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let differentiability samples \((y_i,g_i)\) satisfy \(\|y_i-x\|\le\varepsilon_x\), and define \(H=\operatorname{conv}\{g_i\}\). Compute \(v\in\arg\min_{z\in H}\|z\|\). Declare sampled \((\varepsilon_x,\varepsilon_g)\)-stationarity only when the sampling-adequacy test passes and \(\|v\|\le\varepsilon_g\). A verifiable certificate consists of simplex weights \(\lambda_i\ge0\), \(\sum_i\lambda_i=1\), with \(v=\sum_i\lambda_i g_i\), together with the locality and adequacy data. This is a sampled stopping condition; exact Clarke stationarity requires a consistency or limiting argument as \(\varepsilon_x,\varepsilon_g\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stop when local sampling is adequate and the minimum-norm sampled-hull vector is below tolerance, retaining weights as a certificate.
assumptions_latex: Each \(g_i\) is evaluated at a differentiability point \(y_i\).
The requested tolerances satisfy \(\varepsilon_x,\varepsilon_g\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The data certify sampled \((\varepsilon_x,\varepsilon_g)\)-stationarity, but not automatically exact stationarity.

notation.meaning: minimum-norm point of the sampled hull

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: minimum norm of a sampled gradient hull is the canonical sampled stationarity measure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sampled minimum-norm-hull stopping certificate fits the leaf, but an authoritative source is needed for the stated stopping interface and limiting caveat. The hypotheses must also ensure a nonempty sample set so that H and its minimizer exist; allowing epsilon_x=0 is problematic when gradients are required at differentiability samples near a nonsmooth query.

children.title: Differentiability Detection

knowledge_statements.title: Differentiability Detection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Numerical smooth-stratum test based on gradient agreement and first-order residuals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a query \(x\), nearby differentiability samples \((y_i,f_i,g_i)\), radius \(r>0\), and tolerances \(\tau_g,\tau_f\ge0\), declare the sample set smooth-consistent when \[\max_{i,j}\|g_i-g_j\|\le\tau_g\quad\text{and}\quad \max_{i,j}\frac{|f_i-f_j-g_j^{\mathsf T}(y_i-y_j)|}{\max\{r,\|y_i-y_j\|\}}\le\tau_f.\] Report differentiability detection only as a numerical diagnostic unless these inequalities persist with \(r,\tau_g,\tau_f\downarrow0\) under a sampling-density assumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Treat nearby samples as smooth-consistent when their gradients agree and their pairwise first-order model residuals are uniformly small.
assumptions_latex: \(0<\|y_i-x\|\le r\) for all samples.
Each \(g_i\) is a classical gradient at \(y_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed inequalities define a finite-sample smooth-consistency condition, not a standalone proof of differentiability at \(x\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: gradient clustering plus first-order residuals is a checkable smoothness diagnostic

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Condition is the correct content kind and the statement appropriately calls the test diagnostic rather than conclusive. The residual normalization, threshold scaling, sampling-density requirement, and asserted limiting interpretation are method-specific and have no supporting source.

The sample indices are partitioned into \(q\ge 2\) nonempty candidate clusters.
The sampling-adequacy test passes.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-sample recognition of multiple locally coherent gradient strata.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a query \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), local samples \((y_i,f_i,g_i)\) satisfying \(\|y_i-x\|\le r\), and a partition into \(q\ge2\) nonempty clusters \(I_1,\ldots,I_q\), declare a candidate switching configuration when each cluster satisfies the stated smooth-consistency test with tolerances \((\tau_g,\tau_f)\), the sampling-adequacy test passes, and \[\min_{a\ne b}\left\|\bar g_a-\bar g_b\right\|>\delta,\qquad \bar g_a=|I_a|^{-1}\sum_{i\in I_a}g_i,\] where \(\delta>2\tau_g\). Treat the result only as a finite-sample diagnostic; structural recognition of strata requires additional assumptions or persistent evidence as the sampling radius decreases.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Report a candidate switch when adequate local samples form at least two internally smooth but mutually separated gradient clusters, while treating the result only as a finite-sample diagnostic.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonsmooth-Query Handling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dispatch rule for smooth, switching, and unresolved sampled queries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At query \(x\), collect local differentiability samples and run adequacy, smooth-consistency, and switching-stratum tests. If adequacy fails, add or relocate samples and return no stationarity decision. If smooth-consistency passes without a separated switching configuration, return a representative gradient, such as \(\bar g=m^{-1}\sum_i g_i\). If a switching configuration is recognized, return the convex hull of the cluster representatives and its minimum-norm element. Otherwise shrink the sampling radius or request additional samples. Stop only under the sampled stationarity tolerances or a declared resource limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dispatch adequate queries to a smooth gradient or switching-hull model; otherwise resample, shrink the radius, or report inconclusive.
assumptions_latex: Gradient evaluations are requested only at differentiability points.
Numerical tolerances and a sampling radius are supplied.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure returns a smooth surrogate, a nonsmooth hull surrogate, or an explicit inconclusive status.

notation.meaning: representative gradient in the smooth branch

children.title: False Stationarity from Inadequate Sampling
children.top_down_role: Premature certification caused by missing relevant nearby gradients.

knowledge_statements.title: False Stationarity from Inadequate Sampling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A one-dimensional sampled hull falsely indicates stationarity at a smooth nonstationary query.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(t)=|t|\) and query \(x=1\). Then \(f\) is differentiable at \(x\), with \(\partial_C f(1)=\{1\}\), so \(0\notin\partial_C f(1)\). If an operative sample set improperly includes \(y_1=-1\) and \(y_2=2\), their gradients are \(g_1=-1\) and \(g_2=1\). Hence \[\operatorname{conv}\{g_1,g_2\}=[-1,1],\qquad \min_{v\in[-1,1]}|v|=0.\] The sampled hull therefore reports zero stationarity residual although the query is nonstationary; the failure is caused by a neighborhood crossing the remote kink.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For absolute value at one, samples taken across the kink yield a zero hull residual although the true gradient equals one.
assumptions_latex: The sampled-hull residual is formed from gradients at \(y_1=-1\) and \(y_2=2\).
The query is \(x=1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A zero sampled-hull residual need not imply \(0\in\partial_C f(x)\) when locality or adequacy controls fail.

children.title: Nearly Dependent Sampled Gradients
children.top_down_role: Ill-conditioning from redundant or nearly collinear gradients.

knowledge_statements.title: Nearly Dependent Sampled Gradients
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional conditioning of coefficient-based convex-hull computations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=[g_1,\ldots,g_m]\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}\) have linearly independent columns. Then \(G^{\mathsf T}G\) satisfies \(\kappa_2(G^{\mathsf T}G)=\kappa_2(G)^2=\sigma_{\max}(G)^2/\sigma_{\min}(G)^2\). Hence, if \(\sigma_{\max}(G)\) remains bounded away from zero while \(\sigma_{\min}(G)\to0\), the Gram-system condition number diverges and coefficient recovery becomes increasingly sensitive in relative terms. For coefficients constrained to the probability simplex, absolute coefficient changes remain bounded, although different or substantially changed coefficient representations may correspond to hull points that are close together.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nearly dependent sampled gradients make the Gram system increasingly ill-conditioned. Relative coefficient sensitivity can diverge, although simplex-constrained coefficients remain absolutely bounded and nearby hull points may have substantially different representations.
assumptions_latex: The sampled gradients form a matrix \(G=[g_1,\ldots,g_m]\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}\).
All columns of \(G\) are linearly independent, so \(\sigma_{\min}(G)>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: As \(\sigma_{\min}(G)\downarrow0\) with \(\sigma_{\max}(G)\) bounded away from zero, the Gram-system condition number diverges and relative coefficient sensitivity may become arbitrarily large.

knowledge_statements.title: Unstable Active Support
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coefficient-support instability caused by redundant hull generators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=[-1,1,0]\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times3}\) and minimize \(\lvert G\lambda\rvert^2\) over \(\lambda\geq0\) with \(\mathbf{1}^{\mathsf T}\lambda=1\). Both \(\lambda^{(a)}=(1/2,1/2,0)\) and \(\lambda^{(b)}=(0,0,1)\) attain the unique projected hull point \(G\lambda=0\), but their positive supports are \(\{1,2\}\) and \(\{3\}\), respectively. Thus the projected hull point does not determine the active support, and an algorithm may report different supports solely because it selects different optimal coefficient representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A unique minimum-norm hull point can have multiple coefficient representations with different positive supports, so the reported support can change when an algorithm selects a different optimal representation.
assumptions_latex: Hull points are represented as \(G\lambda\) with \(\lambda\) in the probability simplex.
The positive support is \(\operatorname{supp}_+(\lambda)=\{i:\lambda_i>0\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without uniqueness of the representing coefficients, the active support is not an invariant of the projected hull point.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Memory growth for explicit dense storage of sampled local models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=[g_1,\ldots,g_m]\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}\) contain the retained sampled gradients. Storing \(G\) explicitly requires exactly \(nm\) scalar slots, up to fixed-format metadata of order \(O(m)\). If the hull solver additionally caches the dense Gram matrix \(G^{\mathsf T}G\), storage becomes \(\Theta(nm+m^2)\). knowledge_statements.title: Function-Evaluation Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle-count metric for scalar objective evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a run ending after \(K\) iterations, define its function-evaluation cost by \[N_f:=N_f^{\mathrm{init}}+\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}(s_k+a_k),\] where \(N_f^{\mathrm{init}}\) counts initialization calls, \(s_k\) counts objective values requested to construct the sampled local model, and \(a_k\) counts values requested for trial-point acceptance or other globalization checks. A batched request at \(b\) points contributes \(b\) evaluations to \(N_f\), regardless of parallel execution. Repeated requests are counted again unless an exact cache hit is recognized under the declared reporting protocol.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Function-evaluation cost counts scalar objective-oracle calls used for initialization, sampling, and globalization, including repeated calls unless a declared cache supplies an exact hit; parallel execution does not change the count.
assumptions_latex: A run queries a scalar-value oracle \(x\mapsto f(x)\).
Repeated evaluations are counted unless explicitly served from a declared cache.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The function-evaluation cost is \(N_f=N_f^{\mathrm{init}}+\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}(s_k+a_k)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: When \(g_{m+1}\) is appended, the enlarged Gram matrix is \[\begin{pmatrix}G^{\mathsf T}G&G^{\mathsf T}g_{m+1}\\g_{m+1}^{\mathsf T}G&\lVert g_{m+1}\rVert_2^2\end{pmatrix}.\] Computing its new border requires \(m\) inner products in \(\mathbb{R}^n\), hence \(O(nm)\) arithmetic. children.title: Parallel Sample Evaluation
children.top_down_role: Parallel acquisition of independent local samples.

assumptions_latex: The \(m\) sample-oracle calls are mutually independent once their sample points are fixed.
At most \(p\) identical workers execute calls of uniform cost \(\tau\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The work is \(m\tau\) and the ideal synchronous span is \(\lceil m/p\rceil\tau\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ideal work-span model for independent local oracle calls.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(m\) sample points are fixed before evaluation and each associated oracle call takes time \(\tau\), with no dependencies among calls. The total computational work is \(W=m\tau\). Under synchronous scheduling on \(p\) identical workers, an ideal balanced assignment completes in span \[T_p=\left\lceil\frac{m}{p}\right\rceil\tau.\] Consequently the ideal speedup is at most \(\min\{p,m\}\). Communication, scheduling, unequal oracle times, contention, and serial hull construction can only increase wall-clock time relative to this span; parallel execution does not change the number of oracle evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent sample calls have total work m times their cost and ideal p-worker span equal to ceiling(m/p) times that cost.
knowledge_statements.title: Parallel Sample Evaluation

children.title: Nonsmooth Benchmark Problem Families
children.top_down_role: Academic, finite-max, spectral, constrained, and large-scale test collections.

assumptions_latex: Each benchmark instance specifies an objective, feasible set, starting point, and evaluation interface.
Family labels are assigned from mathematical structure rather than solver behavior.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A benchmark suite is structurally stratified by declared objective, constraint, spectral, and scale attributes.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural classification, not a claim about a particular published collection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonsmooth benchmark family is a collection of fully specified instances grouped by a declared structural attribute. Relevant strata include finite-max problems with \(f(x)=\max_{1\leq i\leq q}f_i(x)\); spectral problems whose objective depends nonsmoothly on eigenvalues or singular values; constrained problems minimizing \(f\) over a specified set \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\); and large-scale problems classified by dimension \(n\), sparsity, or oracle cost. An academic test suite may combine these strata, but every reported instance must state its formulas, dimensions, starting data, constraints, and success criterion so results are reproducible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonsmooth benchmarks should be classified by explicit structure, including finite-max, spectral, constrained, and large-scale families, with reproducible instance data.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonsmooth Benchmark Problem Families

children.title: Solver Comparison Protocols
children.top_down_role: Termination, scaling, acceptance, and performance-reporting conventions.

assumptions_latex: Every solver is run on the same declared instance data and admissible oracle information.
Resource limits and success tolerances are fixed before observing results.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A comparison is protocol-valid only when success, budgets, scaling, acceptance, and reported resource measures are declared uniformly.
review_flags: source needed for a canonical nonsmooth-solver reporting protocol
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum reproducibility condition for comparative computational studies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A solver comparison protocol is admissible when it fixes, before execution: identical problem data and starting points; a scaling convention; a success predicate such as \(r(x)\leq\varepsilon\) together with feasibility requirements; a resource budget \(B\); and uniform rules for failed, timed-out, or numerically invalid runs. It must report objective values, residuals, oracle counts, hull-resource costs, and wall-clock time without conflating these measures. Any solver-specific acceptance or termination test must be mapped to the common success predicate. Aggregated profiles are valid only when their cost ratio and treatment of failures are explicitly defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fair solver comparisons require fixed data, scaling, success tolerances, budgets, failure handling, and separate reporting of oracle, computational, and timing costs.
knowledge_statements.title: Solver Comparison Protocols
